To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

DNA (cytosin-5)-metyltransferase expression is not elevated in human colon tumors compared with normal colon tissue from the same patients, that the concentration of S-adenosylethionine, the methyl group donor, is not reduced below its Km, and that uracil-D NA glycosylase is active in colon tumors.

the level of DNA MTase expression is not significantly increased in colon tumor tissues, that the AdoMet concentration is not significantly reduced, and that the concentration of Adosylhomocysine is not significantly increased, compared with surrounding normal tissue.

DNA (cytosin-5)-mCMTase expression, the concentration ratio of S-adenosymethionine:S-adenosymhomocysteene, and the activity for removing uracil from uracil-DNAs were not altered in human colon cancer tissues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
mechanisms for the development of colon cancer.
the role of DNA methylation and its associated enzymes in colon carcinogenesis.
understanding the role that DNA methylation plays in the development of human cancers, particularly colon cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the mechanism proposed for bacterial MTases does not contribute to human colon cancer development.
the C --> T transitions in colon carcinogenesis are caused primarily by the deamination of methylcytosine.
the C --> T mutations found in the colon are caused by deamination of 5-methyl-cytosine, and not by the mechanism of MTase-mediated deamination of cytosine.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the mechanism we have described for C --> T transitions is not relevant to the etiology of human colon cancer.
the C --> T transitions found in the colon tumors are not due to the mechanism we have proposed.
DNA methylation is involved in colon carcinogenesis, but not by the mechanism proposed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we did not find any evidence for the involvement of the bacterial methyltransferase mechanism in human colon carcinogenesis.
we have found no evidence to support a role for MTase-mediated C --> U deamination as the major cause of these mutations.
the mechanism for the development of C --> T mutations is still not known.
